title: School notices should not become a second job
text: A school notice arrives in a class chat. Another is buried in a diary. A fee deadline belongs to one child, while a consent form belongs to another. For a working parent, the hard part is not reading one message. It is remembering what needs doing, for whom, and by when. Schoolbag turns that scattered information into a family action board, while keeping every important decision with the parent.

title: One notice. Clear next steps.
text: This is the live Schoolbag application. Our demonstration uses synthetic family details and school notices, never real student records. We start with a notice for Kavya. We provide the class, the notice text, and the deadline as written by the school. Schoolbag extracts a first set of actions using transparent rules. These are suggestions to review, not proof that the school has confirmed them. Missing or unclear deadlines remain unresolved instead of being replaced with invented dates.

title: Grounded assistance, visible evidence
text: Now we ask the assistant to review this notice. This is a real Strands agent, using Groq for inference. Its read tool receives only the selected notice context and associated actions. The application requires observed tool execution before accepting the response. The returned advice carries provider and model provenance. It helps summarize obligations and identify useful next steps, but the notice remains the source to check. Model output never signs consent, pays a fee, or sends a message.

title: Parents keep the decision
text: Consider the fee action. The application separates a suggestion from an approved task. An assistant cannot approve it. A parent must review the amount and deadline and explicitly approve before the workflow can continue. In this public demonstration, parent and assistant roles illustrate the authority boundary; they are not verified family identities. We also show that an action can be corrected before completion. Completing the task records a family workflow update. It does not mean that Schoolbag has processed a payment.

title: Two children. One family view.
text: The family board brings Kavya and Arun into the same view, with separate columns and visible pending work. Parents can compare deadlines across children and see potential overlaps. Fee totals make pending amounts easier to review. The calendar export produces a standard calendar file with reminders that can be imported into a calendar application. A WhatsApp reminder remains a draft for the parent to copy and review. Nothing is sent automatically. These small transitions turn reading a notice into a manageable routine.

title: Real infrastructure. Bounded automation.
text: Behind the interface, a React application calls a FastAPI service hosted on Vercel. Neon PostgreSQL persists notices, actions, and workflow history beyond a browser refresh or a local computer shutdown. The Strands advisory path uses a bounded read tool, request budgets, concurrency admission, and explicit error states. Basic pattern redaction reduces common identifiers before inference, but it is not a guarantee that arbitrary personal data is safe to upload. The public demo therefore asks evaluators to use synthetic information.

title: Less chat chaos. More family time.
text: Schoolbag is for families coordinating school life across several streams of information. The value is a clear next action and a visible human decision, not another autonomous system acting on a child's behalf. The working release demonstrates notice intake, grounded assistance, approval, completion, and calendar export. Future work includes stronger identity controls and broader notice formats. Today, the live application and public source let evaluators inspect the workflow themselves.
